We need to prove strong normalization of System F with Nat and primitive recursion under CBV, using a logical relation. This is a hard task. Let me think carefully about the design.

The language is locally nameless for term variables (tm_bvar) and type variables (Ty_BVar) both represented with de Bruijn indices? Wait: open_ty_rec for Ty_BVar uses `if Nat.eqb k i then U else Ty_BVar i`. So Ty_BVar i is a de Bruijn index. But typing uses open_ty T (Ty_FVar X) with locally nameless style and wf_ty with free atom names. The lc_ty_at K T says bound type vars indices < K, and free type variables are atoms. So a "locally closed" type may contain free type variables (atoms) but no dangling de Bruijn indices.

Similarly, terms: tm_bvar de Bruijn indices (term vars), tm_fvar atoms (free vars). Types inside terms are `ty` possibly containing free type atoms; lc_ty_at K T with K = number of bound type variables in scope.

The typing judgment has ty_context Delta : list atom (free type variables in scope), and term context Gamma : list (atom * ty).

The proof: logical relation for strong normalization. Because CBV System F is strongly normalizing. We need a unary type-indexed logical relation.

Complications:
- Terms may contain free term variables? For the fundamental theorem, we interpret typing context Gamma with a substitution/valuation, and terms are closed under that substitution. Since the semantics works with locally nameless style with atoms for free vars, we can define the logical relation on closed terms (no free term vars? or with free vars allowed by environment).

Standard approach: Define an interpretation of contexts: a valuation maps each free term variable x to a term v that is in the interpretation of its type. Then define a term t (possibly with free term variables) to be "in the relation at type T" if for all valuations in the context relation, the substituted term is sn at T. That's the standard "Kripke-style" or "substitution-based" logical relation.

Alternatively, use the more common locally-nameless style logical relation where we define a relation on terms without free variables (locally_closed_tm) and use the "open" operation. The typical System F strong normalization proof (e.g., from TAPL / Software Foundations) uses a logical relation defined with a closing substitution and proves fundamental theorem.

Fixpoint interp (xi : list sem_ty) (T : ty) : sem_ty :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => nth i xi (fun _ => False)
  | Ty_FVar X => fun _ => False
  | Ty_Arrow A B => fun t => lc t ∧ SN t ∧ forall u, interp xi A u -> interp xi B (tm_app t u)
  | Ty_All B => fun t => lc t ∧ SN t ∧ forall U, lc_ty U -> interp (interp xi U :: xi) B (tm_tapp t U)
  | Ty_Nat => fun t => lc t ∧ SN t
  end.

Fixpoint ty_subst_map sigma T :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => Ty_BVar i
  | Ty_FVar X => sigma X
  | Ty_Arrow A B => ...
  | Ty_All B => ...
  | Ty_Nat => ...
  end.

Fixpoint tm_ty_subst_map sigma t :=
  match t with
  | tm_abs T b => tm_abs (ty_subst_map sigma T) (tm_ty_subst_map sigma b)
  | tm_tapp t U => tm_tapp (tm_ty_subst_map sigma t) (ty_subst_map sigma U)
  ...
  end.

Fixpoint tm_subst_all sigma_ty sigma_tm t :=
  match t with
  | tm_fvar x => sigma_tm x
  | tm_abs T b => tm_abs (ty_subst_map sigma_ty T) (tm_subst_all sigma_ty sigma_tm b)
  | ... within tapp type arg, ty_subst_map sigma_ty
  end.

Fixpoint interp (n : nat) : list sem_ty -> ty -> sem_ty :=

```

Fixpoint interp (n : nat) (xi : list sem_ty) (T : ty) {struct T} : sem_ty :=

Actually, the whole function can be written more simply as a single Fixpoint on n where at S n' we define a local fixpoint over T:

```
Fixpoint interp (n : nat) (xi : list sem_ty) (T : ty) {struct n} : sem_ty :=
  match n as n0 return list sem_ty -> ty -> sem_ty with
  | 0 => fun xi T => fun t => lc t
  | S n' =>
      fun xi T =>
        (fix go (T : ty) : sem_ty :=
           match T with
           | Ty_BVar i => fun t => lc t /\ SN t /\ (match nth_error xi i with Some P => P t | None => True end)
           | Ty_FVar X => fun t => lc t /\ SN t
           | Ty_Nat => fun t => lc t /\ SN t
           | Ty_Arrow A B => fun t => lc t /\ SN t /\ (forall u, go A u -> go B (tm_app t u))
           | Ty_All B => fun t => lc t /\ SN t /\ (forall U, ty_closed U -> interp n' (interp n' [] U :: xi) B (tm_tapp t U))
           end) T
  end.
```
Would Coq accept the recursive call `interp n'` inside the local fixpoint `go`? The outer fixpoint's decreasing argument is n; in the branch n = S n', the call interp n' is on a structural subterm of n ✓. The local fixpoint go calls go on A/B (subterms of T, its own decreasing argument T, in the local fixpoint). This should be accepted (nested fixpoint pattern). But the return type of `interp` is `sem_ty = tm -> Prop`, and the match on n returning functions; should be fine.

But there's a subtlety: inside `go`, at the All case, `interp n' (interp n' [] U :: xi) B` — B here is arbitrary and not a subterm of the outer T; that's fine since the decreasing argument n decreases. And `interp n' [] U` with U arbitrary ✓. So positivity/termination fine.

Define `interp (n : nat) (rho : atom -> sem_ty) (T : ty) : sem_ty` by recursion on n and T:
- n = 0: fun t => lc t (base).
- n = S n': match T with
    BVar/FVar/Nat: lc∧SN (plus rho X for FVar)
    Arrow A B: fun t => lc t ∧ SN t ∧ forall u, interp (S n') rho A u -> interp (S n') rho B (app t u)
    All B: fun t => lc t ∧ SN t ∧ forall U, lc_ty U? -> interp n' rho' (open_ty B U) (tapp t U)
  where rho' is the same rho (free atoms), U closed syntactic type.
This is structurally recursive on n (outer) and T (inner); at All, the call interp n' ... (open_ty B U) is on smaller n ✓, and at Arrow, calls interp (S n') on subterms A, B (inner fixpoint on T ✓). Good.

Maybe we can redefine the fuel so that it decreases only at All (impredicative) and not at Arrow, making monotonicity provable? The definition:
```
Fixpoint interp (n : nat) (T : ty) : sem_ty :=
  match n with
  | 0 => lc
  | S n' =>
    (fix go T :=
       match T with
       | Nat => lc∧SN
       | BVar i => False/lc?
       | FVar X => lc? (shouldn't occur)
       | Arrow A B => fun t => lc∧SN∧ forall u, go A u -> go B (app t u)
       | All B => fun t => lc∧SN∧ forall U closed, interp n' (open_ty B U) (tapp t U)
       end) T
  end.
```

Definition LR : ty -> tm -> Prop :=
  fun T t => forall (R : ty -> tm -> Prop), 
    (forall ... closure conditions of R ...) -> R T t.

This is the "candidate" closure: LR is the least relation closed under certain rules (a Church-encoded inductive predicate). The closure conditions include:
- R Nat t if lc t ∧ SN t.
- R (Arrow A B) t if lc t ∧ SN t ∧ forall u, R A u -> R B (app t u).
- R (All B) t if lc t ∧ SN t ∧ forall U, R (open B U) (tapp t U).
As a **closure rule**, the Arrow rule has R A u in a premise — but we're not defining an inductive type; we're using a **Church encoding** where the "closure conditions" are hypotheses of the form `forall T t, (conditions) -> R T t`. The negative occurrence is now inside the hypothesis `forall R, (forall ... R ...) -> R T t`; in Coq, this is just a function type; positivity isn't checked for definitions (only for inductives). So we can define:

Definition LR (T : ty) (t : tm) : Prop :=
  forall (R : ty -> tm -> Prop),
    (forall t, lc t -> SN t -> R Ty_Nat t) ->
    (forall A B t, lc t -> SN t -> (forall u, LR? ...)) -> ...

```
Fixpoint interp (rho : atom -> sem_ty) (xi : list sem_ty) (T : ty) : sem_ty :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => fun t => lc t /\ SN t /\ (match nth_error xi i with Some P => P t | None => False end)
  | Ty_FVar X => fun t => lc t /\ SN t /\ rho X t
  | Ty_Nat => fun t => lc t /\ SN t
  | Ty_Arrow A B => fun t => lc t /\ SN t /\ forall u, interp rho xi A u -> interp rho xi B (app t u)
  | Ty_All B => fun t => lc t /\ SN t /\ forall X P, fresh X B -> fresh X t -> interp (ext rho X P) (P :: xi) B (tapp t (FVar X))
  end.
```
All recursive calls are on subterms A, B ✓. The free-atom env rho is total (atoms are nat, so rho : nat -> sem_ty; no Fresh needed for rho). Freshness conditions: X not free in B and X not free in t. Let's search for another approach: **strong normalization via the "candidates" with the universal type interpreted as an intersection over all candidates and the term-level type application handled by a "semantic type application" relation `R_U` defined *by recursion on the type U* in the fundamental theorem**, not in the LR. The fundamental theorem for T_TAbs needs to prove the All property for all U; if the All clause quantifies over all U and C with `rep U C`, and `rep` is defined as `C = sem U`, then we need sem for all U. But the T_TAbs proof can use the body IH to establish `sem (open B X)` under a suitable environment, and `rep U (sem U)` must hold for all U — this is a lemma "sem is total and correct", proven by induction on U. Let me look at the problem from the **"Nuprl/hereditary substitution"** angle: There's a classic normalization proof for System F by **Tait** that uses **"reducibility candidates"**, and in Coq it's often formalized using **"well-founded recursion on the type with a *stratified* notion where the ∀ type's interpretation is an intersection over all types of a **smaller universe**"**. In Coq's type theory, every type has a universe level; System F's ∀ is impredicative at the level of *syntactic* types, but the logical relation's All clause quantifies over all **closed syntactic types**, which form a `Type`-valued set, not a universe issue. The recursion on syntax is the issue, not universes.

Wait, here's a thought: we can define the LR **by recursion on the type syntax where the All case is not recursive at all** by interpreting the All type as a **"polymorphic" predicate that stores a function from syntactic types to predicates**, and use *the term's type application* only when the term is a `tabs` (a value). For a general term t of All type, the LR can be defined as a predicate on t's **behavior under evaluation to a tabs value**: 
   LR(All B) t := lc t ∧ SN t ∧ forall b v?, t reduces to tabs b (value) -> forall U, LR(open B U)(open_tm_ty b U).
But open B U is still a non-subterm type. However, in this value-based definition, we could define the relation on **values** and use it only for a `tabs b`: LR_all_value(tabs b) := forall U, LR(open B U)(open_tm_ty b U) — still the same non-structural call.
Yet perhaps for the value tabs b, the body term b has a type environment where the bound type variable is abstract; the LR at open B U for the body opened with U is the same as the LR at B under a semantic env P = sem U, and the body IH gives it for all U via the *fundamental theorem at the body's typing derivation*: the body is typed at open B X for a fresh atom X, and the fundamental theorem's IH is applied with sigma[X:=U]. This is exactly what we do; the All clause needs to state the property for all U, but the LR predicate at All can be defined *without* a recursive call on open B U if we define it as a **universal quantification over the term's reducts and over U of the body relation computed by the substitution lemma** — but the predicate would need to mention LR at open B U.

I think the cleanest remaining option is the **semantic-env approach with syntactic substitution avoided**, where the All clause quantifies over a semantic predicate P and a fresh atom, and the *freshness/renaming* is handled by a general equivariance lemma. Let's assess if this avoids impredicative recursion entirely:
  interp rho xi T is a Fixpoint on T (structural), with:
   - All B => fun t => lc∧SN∧ forall X P, X fresh from B and t -> interp (rho[X:=P]) (P::xi) B (tapp t (FVar X)).
  The recursive call is on B (subterm) ✓. No fuel, no impredicative U. The key lemma for T_TApp is a **type-substitution/open lemma** relating interp with env P::xi on B to interp on open_ty B U, but the open_ty shifting issue for ambient env xi arises. However, in the T_TApp case, the All type is a *subterm* of a closed type? The types in the fundamental theorem are wf_ty Delta with free atoms from Delta; after the semantic rho interpretation, types are not closed. The ambient env xi in interp corresponds to binders *inside* the type being interpreted; at the top level xi = []. The open_ty shifting issue arises when we open a binder in a type with outer binders inside it? Let's re-examine: In T_TApp, the type is `Ty_All B` (a subterm of the whole judgment type? The judgment type is exactly Ty_All B for the function term t's type, but the whole term is tapp t U with type open B U). The interp call for IH1 is on the type `Ty_All (sigma B)` with xi = []? In the semantic-env approach, there's no syntactic sigma; IH1 gives interp rho xi0 (Ty_All B) t' where xi0 is the ambient bound-type env from the *context of the judgment*. In the fundamental theorem, the judgment type T may contain free atoms but is lc_ty_at 0 (no free BVars), so no ambient bound env: xi0 = []. Thus IH1 is at xi=[]; the All clause extends to P::[]. The goal type is open_ty B U, which is lc_ty_at 0 (closed w.r.t. BVars) since Ty_All B is lc 0 and U is lc 0. The open_ty lemma for B with xi_high=[] works ✓. The shifting issue for xi_high nonempty would arise if we open a binder inside a type with other binders *outside* the current one but inside the type — e.g., the type Ty_All B where B contains a nested All referencing the outer binder; but open_ty handles nested references to the opened binder correctly (increments k). The xi_high issue in the semantic-env version arises because interp's env xi at a *subterm* includes binders enclosing the subterm; when we call the open lemma on B at the top All, xi=[]; under nested Alls, the open lemma's generalization adds locals. At the top, xi_high = [] because the type being interpreted is a standalone closed-ish type with no BVars at depth 0. But wait, types in the judgment can have *free atoms* but no free BVars, so at the top interp xi=[]; when we descend under a Ty_All inside T, the env grows with locals, and there are no outer binders beyond those locals (since the original type is lc_ty_at 0, all BVars are bound by binders within T; at a subterm under d binders, the env is the d locals, no extra outer xi!). Indeed: interp is called at the top on a type T with lc_ty_at 0 T, and env []; at depth d under binders, the env is exactly the d binders, and T's subterm is lc_ty_at d, so no references beyond the d locals. Therefore xi_high is always empty in interp calls from the fundamental theorem! But the interp Fixpoint's All clause, when the body B has nested binders, recurses with env P::xi where xi = locals; no outer env. Great. So the open lemma only needs xi_high = []; the generalized lemma with locals (inner binders) and no outer binders:

This is the key: with erasure, the impredicative universal quantifier becomes an intersection over all candidates applied to the same term, and the recursion is on the type body. No syntactic U needed. 
  The fundamental theorem for T_TApp: from E(t) ∈ [[∀X.B]] = ⋂_C [[B]]_{X:=C}, instantiate C = [[U]] (the interpretation of U in the current environment) and use the substitution lemma [[B[U]]] = [[B]]_{X:=[[U]]} ✓. The substitution lemma is structural on B: at B's All case, both sides quantify over all candidates C and use the IH on the body with the env extended ✓. At the FVar X case: LHS [[X[U/X]]] = [[U]]; RHS rho[X:=[[U]]](X) = [[U]] ✓.
  T_TAbs: from the body IH for all environments (rho, xi), E(body) ∈ [[B]]_{rho,xi}; for the All semantics need for all candidates C, E(body) ∈ [[B]]_{rho[X:=C], C::xi}. The body's typing has X in the type context; the IH holds for all rho including rho[X:=C], and xi is the de Bruijn env for enclosing type binders; the body's type B is under the binder X, so the env should have C at the head. The IH's statement must be parameterized by an env with a head for the bound X. ✓ Structural.
  The term context valuation: sigma_tm maps free term variables to erased terms related at their types. T_Var ✓; T_Abs: E(abs body) = e_abs (E body) ∈ [[Arrow A B]] iff forall v ∈ [[A]], e_app (e_abs (E body)) v ∈ [[B]]. The body IH gives E(open body x) with x:=v; the erased opening/substitution E(body[v/x]) = e_open (E body) v; and e_app (e_abs (E body)) v --> e_open (E body) v. Need closure of the candidate [[B]] under β-expansion with a value v? In the candidate model, [[Arrow A B]] is defined as a set of terms; its elements are determined by applications. To show e_app (e_abs b) v ∈ [[B]] for v ∈ [[A]], we need the candidate [[B]] to be closed under the β-reduct's reducibility: if e_open b v ∈ [[B]] and v ∈ [[A]] (hence v is SN?), then e_app (e_abs b) v ∈ [[B]]. In the candidate framework, one usually proves [[T]] is a **reducibility candidate**: SN, closed under reduction, and maybe closed under expansion for neutral terms. The β-expansion property for a value argument is provable if [[B]] satisfies the candidate conditions and v is SN: e_app (e_abs b) v reduces to e_open b v and to e_app (e_abs b) v' for v --> v'; by induction on SN v and the candidate's closure properties, expansion holds. This is the standard "CR" proof on erased terms, which is simpler because there are no type steps but still has the same β-expansion structure. However, the candidate intersection definition avoids the impredicativity, so we can prove candidate properties by structural induction on the type with candidates as environments ✓. This is the standard Girard proof! 
  Adequacy: if E(t) ∈ [[T]] for the empty environment, then SN_e(E t) (candidates imply SN), then via the erasure lemma, SN t.

This seems like the *right* path. Let's flesh it out.

Definitions:

Erased terms:
```
Inductive etm : Type :=
  | e_bvar : nat -> etm
  | e_fvar : atom -> etm
  | e_abs : etm -> etm
  | e_app : etm -> etm -> etm
  | e_zero : etm
  | e_succ : etm -> etm
  | e_natrec : etm -> etm -> etm -> etm.
```
Erasure:
```
Fixpoint erase (t : tm) : etm :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar i => e_bvar i
  | tm_fvar x => e_fvar x
  | tm_abs T b => e_abs (erase b)
  | tm_app a b => e_app (erase a) (erase b)
  | tm_tabs b => erase b
  | tm_tapp a T => erase a
  | tm_zero => e_zero
  | tm_succ a => e_succ (erase a)
  | tm_natrec n b s => e_natrec (erase n) (erase b) (erase s)
  end.
```
Erased values: e_abs b, e_zero, e_succ v with numeric value. Define numeric_value_e, value_e.

Erased step:
```
Inductive estep : etm -> etm -> Prop :=
  | E_AppAbs : forall b v, lc_e? value_e v -> e_app (e_abs b) v -->_e e_open b v
  | E_App1 ...
  | E_App2 ...
  | E_Succ ...
  | E_RecArg ...
  | E_RecBase ...
  | E_RecStep ...
  | E_RecZero ...
  | E_RecSucc ...
```
Do we need lc conditions? For SN/erasure, no typing constraints needed; we can define a straightforward CBV step on erased terms. We'll define e_open as substitution of de Bruijn 0 with a term, capture-free, similar to open_tm but on etm. Erasure commutes with open_tm: erase (open_tm t u) = e_open (erase t) (erase u)? Check: open_tm substitutes BVar 0 and increments under abs; erase preserves bvars and abs structure; yes. Also erase (open_tm_ty t U) = erase t (type opening doesn't affect erased bvars/abs structure; open_tm_ty doesn't substitute term vars) ✓. And erase (tm_subst x s t) = e_subst x (erase s) (erase t)? tm_subst replaces fvar x; erase preserves fvars; yes.

Simulation lemma:
```
Lemma erase_step : forall t t', step t t' -> erase t' = erase t \/ estep (erase t) (erase t').

### Erased calculus details

`etm`:
```
Inductive etm : Type :=
  | E_BVar : nat -> etm
  | E_FVar : atom -> etm
  | E_Abs : etm -> etm
  | E_App : etm -> etm -> etm
  | E_Tabs : etm -> etm
  | E_TApp : etm -> etm
  | E_Zero : etm
  | E_Succ : etm -> etm
  | E_Rec : etm -> etm -> etm -> etm.
```
Value:
```
Inductive evalue : etm -> Prop :=
  | ev_abs : forall b, evalue (E_Abs b)
  | ev_tabs : forall b, evalue (E_Tabs b)
  | ev_nat : forall n, enum n -> evalue n
with enum : etm -> Prop := ev_zero | ev_succ n.
```
Actually `value` in the original includes locally_closed_tm for abs/tabs. For the erased calculus, we don't need lc. `value_e` = abs/tabs/numeric.

`e_open_rec k u t` with E_Abs incrementing, E_Tabs not incrementing (type abstraction doesn't bind term vars). e_open t u := e_open_rec 0 u t.
`e_subst x s t` for free term atoms.

Estep:
```
Inductive estep : etm -> etm -> Prop :=
| ES_AppAbs : forall b v, evalue v -> estep (E_App (E_Abs b) v) (e_open b v)
| ES_App1 : forall a a' b, estep a a' -> estep (E_App a b) (E_App a' b)
| ES_App2 : forall v b b', evalue v -> estep b b' -> estep (E_App v b) (E_App v b')
| ES_TAppTabs : forall b, estep (E_TApp (E_Tabs b)) b
| ES_TApp : forall a a', estep a a' -> estep (E_TApp a) (E_TApp a')
| ES_Succ : forall a a', estep a a' -> estep (E_Succ a) (E_Succ a')
| ES_RecArg : forall n n' b s, estep n n' -> estep (E_Rec n b s) (E_Rec n' b s)
| ES_RecBase : forall n b b' s, enum n -> estep b b' -> estep (E_Rec n b s) (E_Rec n b' s)
| ES_RecStep : forall n b s s', enum n -> evalue b -> estep s s' -> estep (E_Rec n b s) (E_Rec n b s')
| ES_RecZero : forall b s, evalue b -> evalue s -> estep (E_Rec E_Zero b s) b
| ES_RecSucc : forall n b s, enum n -> evalue b -> evalue s ->
    estep (E_Rec (E_Succ n) b s) (E_App (E_App s n) (E_Rec n b s)).
```
SN_e:
```
Inductive esn : etm -> Prop := esn_intro : (forall t', estep t t' -> esn t') -> esn t.
```
(No separate lc.)

Erasure E : tm -> etm:
```
Fixpoint erase t :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar i => E_BVar i
  | tm_fvar x => E_FVar x
  | tm_abs T b => E_Abs (erase b)
  | tm_app a b => E_App (erase a) (erase b)
  | tm_tabs b => E_Tabs (erase b)
  | tm_tapp a U => E_TApp (erase a)
  | tm_zero => E_Zero
  | tm_succ a => E_Succ (erase a)
  | tm_natrec n b s => E_Rec (erase n)(erase b)(erase s)
  end.
```
Erasure of open_tm:
  erase (open_tm t u) = e_open (erase t)(erase u)? open_tm_rec increments k under tm_abs, and under tm_tabs? open_tm_rec: tm_tabs t1 => tm_tabs (open_tm_rec k u t1) (k unchanged). e_open_rec: under E_Abs increment k; under E_Tabs unchanged ✓. So yes.
Erasure of open_tm_ty: erase (open_tm_ty t U) = erase t. type opening changes annotations and tapp args but not term structure; erase ignores types. Prove by induction.
Erasure of tm_subst: erase (tm_subst x s t) = e_subst x (erase s)(erase t). tm_subst substitutes fvar x; traverse structure; erase preserves structure/bvars/fvars ✓.
Erasure preserves value: value t -> evalue (erase t). value t = lc abs / lc tabs / numeric. erase(abs)=E_Abs, erase(tabs)=E_Tabs, numeric -> enum.
Erasure preserves numeric: numeric_value t -> enum (erase t).

Now the fundamental theorem context: term substitution sigma : atom -> etm and the term is `esubst sigma t : etm`, which erases and substitutes free atoms. Define esubst:
```
Fixpoint esubst (sigma : atom -> etm) (t : tm) : etm :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar i => E_BVar i
  | tm_fvar x => sigma x
  | tm_abs T b => E_Abs (esubst sigma b)
  | tm_app a b => E_App (esubst sigma a)(esubst sigma b)
  | tm_tabs b => E_Tabs (esubst sigma b)
  | tm_tapp a U => E_TApp (esubst sigma a)
  | tm_zero => E_Zero
  | tm_succ a => E_Succ (esubst sigma a)
  | tm_natrec n b s => E_Rec (esubst sigma n)(esubst sigma b)(esubst sigma s)
  end.
```

Definitions:
- `cand := etm -> Prop`.
- `nth` default. Let's use `nth_error`:
  `Definition env_lookup (env : list cand) (i : nat) : cand := match nth_error env i with Some C => C | None => base_cand end.`
  where base_cand := fun t => elc t ∧ esn t.
  interp:
```
Fixpoint interp (rho : atom -> cand) (xi : list cand) (T : ty) : cand :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => env_lookup xi i
  | Ty_FVar X => rho X
  | Ty_Nat => base_cand
  | Ty_Arrow A B =>
      fun t => elc t /\ esn t /\
        (forall u, interp rho xi A u -> interp rho xi B (E_App t u))
  | Ty_All B =>
      fun t => elc t /\ esn t /\
        (forall (C : cand), is_cand C ->
           interp rho (C :: xi) B (E_TApp t))
  end.
```
  Note: no free-variable env for term variables; terms are erased and may have fvars; interp doesn't care.
  `is_cand` defined before interp? interp's All clause uses is_cand, and is_cand's definition doesn't mention interp, so define is_cand first. It mentions elc, esn, evalue.
  In the All clause, we might want to quantify C over candidates and also require... the env extension C::xi. ✓.
  The `BVar` case uses env_lookup with a default base_cand; for well-scoped types the index is in range.

```coq
(* ===== Erased calculus ===== *)

Inductive etm : Type :=
  | E_BVar : nat -> etm
  | E_FVar : atom -> etm
  | E_Abs : etm -> etm
  | E_App : etm -> etm -> etm
  | E_Tabs : etm -> etm
  | E_TApp : etm -> etm
  | E_Zero : etm
  | E_Succ : etm -> etm
  | E_Rec : etm -> etm -> etm -> etm.

Inductive enum : etm -> Prop :=
  | enum_zero : enum E_Zero
  | enum_succ : forall n, enum n -> enum (E_Succ n).

Inductive evalue : etm -> Prop :=
  | eval_abs : forall b, evalue (E_Abs b)
  | eval_tabs : forall b, evalue (E_Tabs b)
  | eval_nat : forall n, enum n -> evalue n.

Fixpoint numeral_e (n : nat) : etm :=
  match n with O => E_Zero | S m => E_Succ (numeral_e m) end.

Fixpoint e_open_rec (k : nat) (u t : etm) : etm :=
  match t with
  | E_BVar i => if Nat.eqb k i then u else E_BVar i
  | E_FVar x => E_FVar x
  | E_Abs b => E_Abs (e_open_rec (S k) u b)
  | E_App a b => E_App (e_open_rec k u a) (e_open_rec k u b)
  | E_Tabs b => E_Tabs (e_open_rec k u b)
  | E_TApp a => E_TApp (e_open_rec k u a)
  | E_Zero => E_Zero
  | E_Succ a => E_Succ (e_open_rec k u a)
  | E_Rec n b s => E_Rec (e_open_rec k u n) (e_open_rec k u b) (e_open_rec k u s)
  end.

Definition e_open (t u : etm) : etm := e_open_rec 0 u t.

Inductive estep : etm -> etm -> Prop :=
  | ES_AppAbs : forall b v, evalue v -> estep (E_App (E_Abs b) v) (e_open b v)
  | ES_App1 : forall a a' b, estep a a' -> estep (E_App a b) (E_App a' b)
  | ES_App2 : forall v b b', evalue v -> estep b b' -> estep (E_App v b) (E_App v b')
  | ES_TAppTabs : forall b, estep (E_TApp (E_Tabs b)) b
  | ES_TApp : forall a a', estep a a' -> estep (E_TApp a) (E_TApp a')
  | ES_Succ : forall a a', estep a a' -> estep (E_Succ a) (E_Succ a')
  | ES_RecArg : forall n n' b s, estep n n' -> estep (E_Rec n b s) (E_Rec n' b s)
  | ES_RecBase : forall n b b' s, enum n -> estep b b' -> estep (E_Rec n b s) (E_Rec n b' s)
  | ES_RecStep : forall n b s s', enum n -> evalue b -> estep s s' -> estep (E_Rec n b s) (E_Rec n b s')
  | ES_RecZero : forall b s, evalue b -> evalue s -> estep (E_Rec E_Zero b s) b
  | ES_RecSucc : forall n b s, enum n -> evalue b -> evalue s ->
      estep (E_Rec (E_Succ n) b s) (E_App (E_App s n) (E_Rec n b s)).

Inductive esn : etm -> Prop :=
  | esn_intro : forall t, (forall t', estep t t' -> esn t') -> esn t.
```

Erased local closure:
```coq
Inductive elc_at : nat -> etm -> Prop :=
  | elc_bvar : forall k i, i < k -> elc_at k (E_BVar i)
  | elc_fvar : forall k x, elc_at k (E_FVar x)
  | elc_abs : forall k b, elc_at (S k) b -> elc_at k (E_Abs b)
  | elc_app : forall k a b, elc_at k a -> elc_at k b -> elc_at k (E_App a b)
  | elc_tabs : forall k b, elc_at k b -> elc_at k (E_Tabs b)
  | elc_tapp : forall k a, elc_at k a -> elc_at k (E_TApp a)
  | elc_zero : forall k, elc_at k E_Zero
  | elc_succ : forall k a, elc_at k a -> elc_at k (E_Succ a)
  | elc_rec : forall k n b s, elc_at k n -> elc_at k b -> elc_at k s -> elc_at k (E_Rec n b s).
Hint Constructors elc_at enum evalue : core.
Definition elc t := elc_at 0 t.
```

Erasure:
```coq
Fixpoint erase (t : tm) : etm :=
  match t with
  | tm_bvar i => E_BVar i
  | tm_fvar x => E_FVar x
  | tm_abs T b => E_Abs (erase b)
  | tm_app a b => E_App (erase a) (erase b)
  | tm_tabs b => E_Tabs (erase b)
  | tm_tapp a U => E_TApp (erase a)
  | tm_zero => E_Zero
  | tm_succ a => E_Succ (erase a)
  | tm_natrec n b s => E_Rec (erase n) (erase b) (erase s)
  end.
```

Let's add to sol.v:

```coq
(* ================= Candidate model ================= *)

Definition cand := etm -> Prop.

Definition base_cand : cand := fun t => elc t /\ esn t.

Definition is_cand (C : cand) : Prop :=
  (forall t, C t -> elc t /\ esn t) /\
  (forall t t', C t -> estep t t' -> C t') /\
  (forall t, elc t -> ~ evalue t -> (forall t', estep t t' -> C t') -> C t).

Lemma base_cand_is_cand : is_cand base_cand.
Proof.
  unfold is_cand, base_cand. repeat split.
  - intros t [H1 H2]. auto.
  - intros t t' [H1 H2] Hs. split; [apply estep_pres_elc with t; assumption|apply esn_step with t; assumption].
  - intros t Hl Hnv Hred. split; [assumption|constructor; intros t' Hs; apply Hred in Hs; destruct Hs; assumption].
Qed.
```

Then `env_lookup` and `interp`:
```coq
Definition env_lookup (xi : list cand) (i : nat) : cand :=
  match nth_error xi i with Some C => C | None => base_cand end.

Fixpoint interp (rho : atom -> cand) (xi : list cand) (T : ty) : cand :=
  match T with
  | Ty_BVar i => env_lookup xi i
  | Ty_FVar X => rho X
  | Ty_Nat => base_cand
  | Ty_Arrow A B => fun t =>
      elc t /\ esn t /\ (forall u, interp rho xi A u -> interp rho xi B (E_App t u))
  | Ty_All B => fun t =>
      elc t /\ esn t /\ (forall C, is_cand C -> interp rho (C :: xi) B (E_TApp t))
  end.
```
Note: the All clause uses `C :: xi` with C at the front. The open lemma env convention derived earlier: opened binder at position k=length locals, with env locals ++ [C]. Let's verify with this All clause: at body T under env [C] at top (xi=[]); under an inner All in T, env D::[C] = D :: ([] ++ [C]) = [D] ++ [C] ✓ locals=[D]. The interp All clause prepends D: env D :: xi_current where xi_current=[C] ✓. So env = locals ++ [C] with locals as the front list in order innermost-first. open_ty_rec k replaces the binder at index k, matching position k in the env (locals length k, then C) ✓. Great.
